input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?

input.answer: The project avoided frequent re-centering because backtests showed the extra fees were outweighed by impermanent loss and swap costs. This effect persisted even in flat regimes where narrowing theoretically has an edge, leading to the conclusion that "Wąskie pasmo to short gamma" and that active re-centering realized divergence losses rather than capturing alpha.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: In an uptrend, the LP position drifts out of its liquidity range as the asset price rises. Arbitrageurs then trade against the position at a stale price, realizing the loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR). This loss typically exceeds the fees earned because the position is no longer optimally positioned to capture organic flow. In a flat market, the price stays within the range, allowing the LP to collect fees without suffering significant LVR, making the strategy profitable relative to HODL.

verdict.correctnessReason: The answer captures the out-of-range drift and the attribution of losses to LVR. It misses the reference's key points that fee yield scales with range width and that the journal has no live measurement of fees in an uptrend, and it frames the result as LVR exceeding fees rather than lower fees.

input.question: Why did the bot and its API server run on the Windows machine rather than on the Mac I was working on?
input.reference: The bot had to run 24/7 (nightly pipeline, 07:30 report, Telegram alerts), so the owner's always-on Windows desktop became the server with the Mac and iPhone as clients over LAN and VPN; the docs add that a closed laptop would mean a dead autopilot.
input.answer: The Windows machine was chosen because it could run the bot and API server 24/7 as headless Windows services (NSSM) that start at boot and survive crashes, with sleep disabled and power-on after loss set in BIOS. input.question: Why did the bot never open, close or re-range positions on its own, and was automatic execution possible at all?
input.reference: The bot ran in PROPOSE mode with no wallet key on the server, so the owner signed every transaction; the only cost was signing delay (up to ~13 h at night, ~61 h over a weekend), measured from day one, and AUTO existed only as a later rung of the trust path OBSERVE-PROPOSE-AUTO that was deliberately not enabled at the start.
input.answer: The bot operated exclusively in PROPOSE mode, meaning it "executes nothing on its own." While it generated proposals for opening, rebalancing, or closing positions, these required manual approval and signature via a browser wallet (Rabby). Full automatic execution (AUTO mode) was planned but "never enabled" and "not built." Consequently, the bot could not independently open, close, or re-range positions; all actions were semi-automatic, requiring human intervention for the final transaction signature.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: In an uptrend, a concentrated-range LP earns fewer fees than in a flat market because the price quickly exits the narrow range, ending the fee-earning period. The journal notes that in UP windows the strategy loses (e.g., "okna UP = klęska") and that narrow strategies "umiera na IL od trendu" (die from LVR) rather than accumulating fees. In FLAT, the price stays within the range longer, so the LP can harvest more organic trading volume. The LVR mechanism—loss to arbitrageurs at stale prices on every market move—means the wider the price moves, the more the LP loses relative to HODL, while flat conditions allow fees to accumulate without the price leaving the range.

wąska zbiera więcej fees ($1,316) ale umiera na IL od trendu
the loss to arbitrageurs who trade against the position at a stale price on every market move

verdict.correctnessReason: The answer gives the reference's core mechanism (fees accrue only in range, so a narrow range is left behind in a trend but stays in range in a flat market) and attributes up-window losses to IL/LVR, though it omits the width/fee-yield trade-off and the lack of a live measurement.

input.question: What does the function fetchFreshPool do?

input.answer: fetchFreshPool (in src/utils/uniswap.ts) fetches the current on-chain pool state via factory.getPool, then reads slot0 and liquidity to build a new Pool object with the same tokens and fee tier. input.answer: The bot and API server were run on a home Windows machine because a browser cannot serve as the automation engine; a closed laptop would result in a "dead autopilot" {"chunkId": "docs/UI-DESIGN.md:35", "quote": "the browser cannot be the automation engine — a closed laptop means a dead autopilot"}. The project vision originally suggested a small VPS, but ultimately, a "home Windows machine running 24/7 took that role" {"chunkId": "docs/UI-DESIGN.md:35", "quote": "a home Windows machine running 24/7 took that role"}. This setup allowed the bot to run as a separate 24/7 Node daemon {"chunkId": "docs/UI-DESIGN.md:35", "quote": "The bot is a separate process"}.

input.question: Why did the bot never open, close or re-range positions on its own, and was automatic execution possible at all?
input.reference: The bot ran in PROPOSE mode with no wallet key on the server, so the owner signed every transaction; the only cost was signing delay (up to ~13 h at night, ~61 h over a weekend), measured from day one, and AUTO existed only as a later rung of the trust path OBSERVE-PROPOSE-AUTO that was deliberately not enabled at the start.
input.answer: The bot never executed actions on its own because the full-automation phase (Phase 4) was not built as planned; the "AUTO mode was never enabled" {"chunkId": "docs/PLAN.md:151", "quote": "AUTO mode was never enabled"}. Instead, the system implemented semi-automatic execution (Phase 3), where signals result in a "ready transaction" that requires a "signature in Rabby" {"chunkId": "docs/PLAN.md:151", "quote": "semi-automatic execution (signal \u2192 ready transaction \u2192 signature in Rabby)"}. Regarding specific actions, the "on signal" mechanism was designed to "PROPOSE: a proposal for approval" rather than providing direct execution {"chunkId": "docs/UI-DESIGN.md:50", "quote": "PROPOSE: a proposal for approval"}. Furthermore, automatic execution for "ROTATE" actions was not supported because the existing rebalance builder only handled single-pool scenarios {"chunkId": "journal/CONTEXT.md:2673", "quote": "planRebalance() bierze jeden Pool na wejściu (zakłada, że stara i nowa pozycja są w TEJ SAMEJ puli)"}.

input.question: Why was a crypto/crypto pair (cbBTC/WETH) considered riskier than a crypto/stable pair?
input.reference: It was not riskier as an LP: against HODL cbBTC/WETH was the best pool (365 d: +11.42 for k2h24, the largest LP-vs-HODL alpha; 27.08 closest to passing the gate; on 720 d the only pool with 65% winning windows), but in USD it carries full crypto beta with no stable cushion (HODL -51.5% APR, max drawdown 61.5%), so LP and HODL lose together.
input.answer: A crypto/crypto pair like cbBTC/WETH was considered riskier because it carries "pełna beta krypto" (full crypto beta), meaning there is "ŻADNEJ poduszki stable" (no stable cushion) to offset volatility {"chunkId": "journal/CONTEXT.md:3806", "quote": "obie nogi crypto = pełna beta, ŻADNEJ poduszki stable"}. In contrast, a crypto/stable pair such as WETH/USDC provides a "poduszka" (cushion) where the stable leg mitigates downside risk {"chunkId": "journal/KAPITAL-REKOMENDACJA.md:33", "quote": "stable = poduszka"}. Consequently, during a bearish regime, the cbBTC/WETH pair can face extreme drawdowns (e.g., maxDD of 61.5%) because it lacks the protection offered by a stablecoin leg {"chunkId": "journal/CONTEXT.md:3806", "quote": "maxDD 61.5%!"}.

stable = poduszka

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: In an uptrend, concentrated liquidity provides fee income that is offset by the cost of its convexity. Because LPs "sell into rallies and buy into drawdowns," a trending year can result in costs that "cost more than fees earn" {"chunkId": "docs/CASE-STUDY.md:105", "quote": "you sell into rallies and buy into drawdowns, and in a trending year that costs more than fees earn"}. Additionally, strategies like the "no-swap" variant fail in rising markets because, after losing the upper boundary, the position remains in USDC and "in a rising market misses the move" {"chunkId": "journal/CONTEXT.md:1362#p9", "quote": "w rynku rosnącym przegapi ruch tak samo skutecznie"}. In some cases, the loss of value from impermanent loss and re-centering can significantly exceed the fees collected {"chunkId": "journal/CONTEXT.md:1362#p7", "quote": "IL i re-centering zjadły ~$1.9k (cbBTC) i ~$2.9k (base-030) ponad to, co dołożyły fee"}.

input.question: What infrastructure problems were there, was anything changed on the production machine while the capital was already invested, and when?

input.answer:
Infrastructure problems included a volatility estimator that measured pool microstructure rather than the asset, resulting in "broken units" for calibration (docs/CASE-STUDY.md:44). Additionally, a UI error caused a rebalance attempt to revert due to a stale pool state (docs/CASE-STUDY.md:67), and a sampling gap caused a $35 drift in the tranche balance (docs/CASE-STUDY.md:67).

The production `SIGMA_MODE` was changed from `swap` to `grid15` because `SIGMA_MODE` had not been set anywhere, causing the live bot to use the wrong estimator (journal/CONTEXT.md:1362#p4). This change was implemented via a service restart at 10:15:53Z to ensure subsequent narrowing used the correct sigma (journal/CONTEXT.md:1362#p4).

input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: Active re-centering (narrowing) was avoided because it failed to outperform passive wide ranges in backtests, particularly over a 720-day period. While narrowing generated significantly higher fees, the resulting Impermanent Loss (IL) from frequent re-balancing outweighed those gains. Specifically, for cbBTC and base-030, re-centering costs (IL) consumed approximately $1.9k and $2.9k respectively, more than the additional fees provided. This occurred because a narrow band acts as "short gamma," where every re-centering "REALIZUJE dywergencję" (realizes divergence). Additionally, narrowing proved ineffective even in "flat" market regimes, where passive wide ranges maintained higher win rates and better performance. The strategy instead prioritized a "wide passive LP" approach.

input.question: Why did the bot never open, close or re-range positions on its own, and was automatic execution possible at all?
input.reference: The bot ran in PROPOSE mode with no wallet key on the server, so the owner signed every transaction; the only cost was signing delay (up to ~13 h at night, ~61 h over a weekend), measured from day one, and AUTO existed only as a later rung of the trust path OBSERVE-PROPOSE-AUTO that was deliberately not enabled at the start.
input.answer: The bot did not execute actions automatically because the "AUTO mode was never enabled" and Phase 4 (full-auto execution) was "Not built as planned" (docs/PLAN.md:151). Instead, the system functioned as "semi-automatic execution," where signals generated "ready transaction" sequences that required a "signature in Rabby" (docs/PLAN.md:151). For specific actions like "on signal," the mechanism was designed to "PROPOSE: a proposal for approval," whereas full "AUTO" execution was not built (docs/UI-DESIGN.md:50). Additionally, for "ROTATE" actions, the automatic "[Zatwierdź]" (Approve) feature did not work because the existing rebalance builder only supported single-pool operations, whereas rotation requires handling different pools (journal/CONTEXT.md:2673).

input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: We kept the ranges wide because the data showed that moving them to stay near the price (“active re‑centering”) did not improve, and in fact hurt, performance.  Re‑centering with swap costs was already essentially free (`recenter:'noswap'` in flatOnlyLP), so there was no incentive to keep the range tight.  In backtests extending the window to 720 days killed the strategy; zero of 21 configurations passed the gate, and in the 365‑day data the passive wide range yielded HODL + fees − IL, while the narrow ranges added variance without expectation (see the “narrowing added variance without adding expectancy” finding).  The live experiment (31 Aug → 11 Sep) confirmed this: a narrow range earned only ≈$8.6 in fees, then closed at −$32 versus HODL, exactly as the back‑tests predicted.  Because narrowing grew fees but also increased impermanent loss and drawdown, the decision was to stay with wide passive ranges and only consider narrowing in a confirmed flat episode.

input.answer: Crypto/crypto pairs (e.g., cbBTC/WETH) are riskier because both legs are subject to the same market volatility, so the pool has no stable‑asset cushion. In contrast, a crypto/stable pair uses a stable‑asset leg that acts as a buffer, providing diversification and protecting the pool from the full‑market beta of the crypto side.

input.answer: The 365‑day backtests were run on a single, largely sideways‑to‑down year. The volatility estimator was calibrated on that short window, so the σ values were very low and the narrow ranges were optimal for that regime. When the window was extended to 720 days, the data set included a strong up‑trend and a wider range of volatility patterns. The same σ‑based calibration now produced ranges that were too narrow for the longer, more volatile history, leading to many losses in the “up” regimes and causing every configuration to fail the multi‑regime gate. In short, the short window over‑fitted to a quiet period; the longer window exposed the true risk profile and eliminated the apparent profitability.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: During up‑trends the LP’s concentrated ranges frequently evaporated from the market, forcing the bot to rebalance and sell into rising prices.  Re‑balancing consumes swap and gas costs and the short‑gamma position sells into the rally, so fee collection drops dramatically.  In a flat market the ranges stay in‑range for almost the whole period, producing high fee‑to‑cost ratios: for ±5 % the fee income was 4× higher than for the wide passive range and the re‑centering cost was negligible.  The back‑tests show that in up‑trends the LP earned only a fraction of the flat‑market fees, because the active re‑balancing required swaps (swaps+gas ≈ $1.9 k for cbBTC, $2.9 k for base‑030) that surpassed the fee revenue.  In contrast, flat episodes kept the LP in‑range and the high fee income was not offset by swap costs.

input.question: Why did we keep the capital commitment small even though ETH and BTC were rising?
input.reference: Tranche 1 ($6 092) was planned as a first stage and run as an operational experiment on a calibration the team itself considered broken (720 d: 0/21), the entry after an ETH +25%/90d pump was recorded with an explicit FOMO note, and on 02.09 the product failed to beat HODL in all five measurements, so the planned scale-up never happened.
input.answer:
The capital commitment was kept small because the LP strategy is not designed to outperform in a rising market.

The Monte Carlo work showed the strategy’s asymmetry: it wins in calm by fees, but in a rise it underperforms HODL because the pool sells the rising asset. The verdict written down is that "przy wzroście zarabiamy MNIEJ niż HODL" and the product is "HODL+yield−drag" with "przy płaskim rynku realistycznie 8–12%/r z prowizji"; the value is measurement and research, not alpha.

That assessment led to a deliberate small scale. The 24.09 review was to decide "Decyzja o skali/sensie na przeglądzie 24.09" and the GM v2 test carried the exposure limit "limit ekspozycji jak w E7 krok 2 (≤25% transzy) obowiązuje".

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?

The case study explicitly says concentrated liquidity in trending markets sells into rallies and buys into drawdowns. That convex payoff costs more than fees earn.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer:
The project treats narrow ranges as *short gamma*: each re-centering in a trend *realises* the divergence between the pool and HODL, i.e. it locks in losses faster than fees can compensate.

* In the 720d walk-forward, narrowing earned *more fees* but finished lower because IL and re-centring consumed the extra income:
  * “mechanism … narrowing earned a LOT more fees — cbBTC $2169 vs $541 … and finished LOWER. … IL and re-centering ate ~$1.9k … above what fees added, at 65 … rebalances. Narrow range is short gamma: each posture transition REALISES divergence.”
  * “the whole chain … stood on EV that ignored the main cost.”

* More generally, “for ETH/stable and ETH/BTC pairs, concentrated liquidity did not beat HODL 50/50 out of sample. The fee income is real but it is paid for with convexity: you sell into rallies and buy into drawdowns, and in a trending year that costs more than fees earn.”

* In an uptrend the strategy is especially penalised:
  * “In uptrend: up 0% won, avg −13.91 … For comparison variant WITH swap in up: −3.14 — also bad, but almost 3× less painful.”
  * “In uptrend the strategy sells ETH and buys USDC; in a rising market that underperforms HODL.”
  * “The narrowing experiment … sat in range for 11 days and earned ≈ $8.6 in fees, then the trend breaker closed it at −$32 versus HODL.”

Hence in an uptrend the LP underperforms HODL and the extra fees collected by narrowing are more than offset by realised IL/price divergence, whereas in a flat market the pool stays in-range, IL is symmetric and small, so fee income is retained.

Czyli IL i re-centering zjadły ~$1.9k (cbBTC) i ~$2.9k (base-030) ponad to, co dołożyły fee, przy 65 i 88 rebalansach. Wąskie pasmo to short gamma: każde przejście postury REALIZUJE dywergencję.
The fee income is real but it is paid for with convexity: you sell into rallies and buy into drawdowns, and in a trending year that costs more than fees earn.
up 0% wygranych, śr. −13.91, najgorsze −17.86
Dla porównania wariant ZE swapem w up: −3.14 — też słabo, ale prawie 3× mniej boleśnie.
